lessonTitle: Glomerular Filtration and Renal Blood Flow

blocks.text: A laboratory reports a serum creatinine of 120 micromol/L. In a muscular 25-year-old man that may be a mild concern; in a frail 85-year-old woman it may mean her kidneys are working at well under half their normal capacity. To read that number properly you must understand what the glomerulus filters, how fast it filters, and how the kidney defends that rate.

blocks.markdown: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. Urine formation begins in the **glomerulus**, a tuft of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule, where about a fifth of the plasma flowing through is forced across a filtration barrier into the capsular space. Total renal blood flow is about 1.1 L/min (roughly 20 to 25 per cent of cardiac output) and renal plasma flow about 600 mL/min. The **filtration fraction**, GFR divided by renal plasma flow, is about 0.2.

blocks.title: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)
blocks.text: GFR is the volume of plasma filtered across all glomeruli per unit time. In a healthy young adult it is about 120 to 125 mL/min per 1.73 square metres of body surface, roughly 180 litres per day, and it falls with age. The filtrate is essentially plasma without cells and with almost no protein; almost all of it is reabsorbed later in the nephron.

rows: Fenestrated (pores about 70 to 100 nm) with no diaphragm, covered by a negatively charged surface layer
Blood cells and platelets; fenestrae are too large to hold back proteins on size alone
Fused basement membranes of endothelium and podocytes: type IV collagen, laminin and negatively charged heparan sulfate proteoglycans
Large molecules by size, and anionic (negatively charged) proteins such as albumin by charge repulsion
Interdigitating foot processes separated by filtration slits bridged by a slit diaphragm containing nephrin
Fine size selectivity: the final barrier to macromolecules, and anchoring of the filter
blocks.caption: The three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier.

blocks.markdown: The barrier is selective by both **size** and **charge**. Water, ions, glucose, amino acids and urea pass freely. Molecules with an effective radius above about 4 nm are largely excluded, and for a given size, negatively charged molecules are filtered less than neutral or positive ones. Albumin (about 66 kDa, effective radius about 3.5 nm and negatively charged) is therefore filtered only in tiny amounts. If the charge barrier or podocyte structure is damaged, albumin leaks into the urine (albuminuria or proteinuria); if the barrier is physically disrupted, red cells may appear (haematuria).

blocks.caption: Starling forces across the glomerulus: Kf is the filtration coefficient (permeability times area); PGC is glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, PBS is Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure and piGC is glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (Bowman's space oncotic pressure is negligible).

blocks.title: Net filtration pressure and GFR
blocks.prompt: In a healthy glomerulus PGC = 55 mmHg, PBS = 15 mmHg and piGC = 30 mmHg (mean values along the capillary). If Kf = 12.5 mL/min per mmHg, calculate the net filtration pressure and the GFR.

steps.text: Hydrostatic pressure in the capillary pushes fluid out; the pressure in Bowman's space and the oncotic pressure of plasma proteins oppose filtration.

blocks.answer: Net filtration pressure is 10 mmHg and GFR is 125 mL/min, in agreement with the normal value of about 120 to 125 mL/min.

blocks.title: Why creatinine estimates GFR
blocks.text: Creatinine is produced by muscle at a fairly constant rate, is freely filtered, is not reabsorbed, and is secreted only slightly by the tubules. Almost everything filtered is therefore excreted, so its clearance approximates GFR. Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. A small tubular secretion makes creatinine clearance slightly overestimate true GFR.

blocks.caption: Creatinine clearance: Ucr is urine creatinine concentration, V is urine flow rate (mL/min), Pcr is plasma creatinine concentration. Ucr and Pcr must be in the same units.

blocks.title: Creatinine clearance from a timed urine collection
blocks.prompt: A patient has plasma creatinine 90 micromol/L (0.090 mmol/L), urine creatinine 6.0 mmol/L and a urine flow of 1.5 mL/min. Estimate GFR.

steps.text: Both creatinine concentrations are in mmol/L, so they can be used directly. Multiply urine concentration by flow: 6.0 x 1.5 = 9.0 mmol/min equivalent (units cancel later).
Interpret: this is below the typical young adult value of about 120, which may be normal for an older adult or may indicate reduced function depending on age.

blocks.markdown: The kidney must keep GFR steady despite the fall in arterial pressure on standing or rise during exercise. **Autoregulation** keeps renal blood flow and GFR nearly constant when mean arterial pressure varies between roughly 80 and 180 mmHg. Two mechanisms act on the **afferent arteriole**. The **myogenic response** makes the smooth muscle constrict when stretched by higher pressure and relax when pressure falls. **Tubuloglomerular feedback** uses the macula densa cells of the distal tubule: if GFR rises, more sodium chloride reaches them, and they signal the nearby afferent arteriole to constrict (adenosine is involved), lowering PGC and GFR back towards normal. Below the range, GFR falls with pressure.

blocks.caption: Effects of altering afferent or efferent arteriolar resistance. With very severe efferent constriction GFR eventually falls because plasma flow becomes too low.

blocks.title: Limits of serum creatinine
blocks.text: Serum creatinine depends on muscle mass as well as GFR, so it is low in small or frail people and high in muscular people. Because creatinine production is roughly constant, steady-state serum creatinine rises as GFR falls, but the relationship is inverse and not linear: halving GFR approximately doubles the serum level, so early loss of function can be hidden within the reference range.

points: The filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated capillary endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms; it selects by size and by negative charge.
GFR (about 120 to 125 mL/min) equals Kf times the net filtration pressure; creatinine clearance, Ucr x V / Pcr, estimates it because creatinine is freely filtered and barely handled by tubules.
Autoregulation by the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback adjusts afferent arteriolar tone to hold renal blood flow and GFR steady over a mean arterial pressure of about 80 to 180 mmHg.
Efferent constriction raises GFR but lowers renal blood flow; afferent constriction lowers both.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier in the order a molecule meets them when moving from blood to Bowman's space?

options.text: Podocyte foot processes, basement membrane, capillary endothelium
Fenestrated capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms
Glomerular basement membrane, capillary endothelium, mesangial cells
Tubular epithelium, basement membrane, capillary endothelium

questions.correctOptionText: Fenestrated capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms

distractorRationale.a: This is the reverse order, from Bowman's space to blood.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: blood meets the endothelium first, then the GBM, then the podocyte slit diaphragms.
distractorRationale.c: The endothelium comes before the basement membrane, and mesangial cells are not a layer of the barrier.
distractorRationale.d: Tubular epithelium is not part of the glomerular filtration barrier.

questions.explanation: Filtered fluid crosses the fenestrated endothelium, then the glomerular basement membrane, and finally the filtration slits between podocyte foot processes bridged by slit diaphragms. Each layer contributes to size and charge selectivity.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child has swollen eyelids and urine that is persistently frothy. Urinalysis shows heavy protein loss (mainly albumin) but no red cells. Which property of the filtration barrier is most likely to be lost in this child's disease?

options.text: The fenestrae of the endothelium, so that red cells escape
The negative charge and podocyte structure that normally restrict albumin
The macula densa signalling that adjusts afferent arteriolar tone
The permeability of the tubule to creatinine

questions.correctOptionText: The negative charge and podocyte structure that normally restrict albumin

distractorRationale.a: Escape of red cells (haematuria) is not present, and fenestrae do not restrict proteins by size anyway.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: loss of charge selectivity and podocyte function lets albumin, a negatively charged protein, cross the barrier.
distractorRationale.c: Macula densa signalling controls GFR autoregulation, not albumin filtration.
distractorRationale.d: Tubular creatinine handling is unrelated to protein leakage into the urine.

questions.explanation: Albumin is largely held back by the combination of its size and its negative charge, which is repelled by the anionic basement membrane and slit diaphragm. Heavy albuminuria without haematuria points to loss of this selectivity, particularly at the level of the podocytes and charge barrier.

questions.stem: A patient has a plasma creatinine of 0.12 mmol/L, a urine creatinine of 9.0 mmol/L and a urine flow rate of 1.2 mL/min. Calculate the creatinine clearance in mL/min.
questions.explanation: Creatinine clearance is Ucr x V / Pcr = 9.0 x 1.2 / 0.12 = 90 mL/min. Because creatinine is freely filtered and barely secreted or reabsorbed, this approximates the GFR.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection from a 50-year-old man has a volume of 1.8 L and a creatinine concentration of 7.0 mmol/L. His plasma creatinine is 0.10 mmol/L. Calculate his creatinine clearance in mL/min (take 24 hours as 1440 minutes).
questions.explanation: Urine flow is 1800 mL / 1440 min = 1.25 mL/min. Clearance is 7.0 x 1.25 / 0.10 = 87.5 mL/min, which approximates his GFR.

questions.stem: A patient's GFR falls from 120 to 60 mL/min and creatinine production is constant. Assuming a new steady state is reached, what happens to serum creatinine?

options.text: It remains unchanged
It halves
It approximately doubles
It rises about four-fold

distractorRationale.a: Serum creatinine must rise until excretion again matches production.
distractorRationale.b: A fall in GFR reduces excretion, so serum creatinine rises, not falls.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: at steady state production equals GFR x plasma concentration, so halving GFR requires plasma concentration to double.
distractorRationale.d: A four-fold rise would correspond to a quarter of the original GFR.

questions.explanation: At steady state, creatinine excreted (GFR x Pcr) equals creatinine produced, which is constant. If GFR halves, Pcr must double to keep excretion equal to production, showing the inverse relationship and why early GFR loss can hide within the reference range.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, mean arterial pressure rises from 100 to 140 mmHg during a stressful exercise test, yet GFR changes very little. What is the principal reason?

options.text: The afferent arteriole constricts, limiting the rise in glomerular capillary pressure
The efferent arteriole dilates, increasing filtration
The filtration coefficient Kf rises in proportion to pressure
The kidneys stop filtering until pressure returns to baseline

questions.correctOptionText: The afferent arteriole constricts, limiting the rise in glomerular capillary pressure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback increase afferent resistance, buffering PGC.
distractorRationale.b: Efferent dilation would lower PGC and GFR but is not the main autoregulatory response to raised pressure.
distractorRationale.c: Kf does not rise in proportion to pressure and would worsen, not stabilise, filtration.
distractorRationale.d: Filtration does not stop; it is held at a near-constant rate.

questions.explanation: When arterial pressure rises, afferent arteriolar smooth muscle is stretched and constricts, and tubuloglomerular feedback reinforces this. The extra resistance upstream of the glomerulus absorbs the pressure rise, so PGC, and therefore GFR, stay nearly constant within the autoregulatory range.

questions.stem: Which change in arteriolar tone would be expected to increase GFR while decreasing renal blood flow?

options.text: Afferent arteriolar constriction
Afferent arteriolar dilation
Mild efferent arteriolar constriction
Efferent arteriolar dilation

distractorRationale.a: This lowers both PGC and renal blood flow, so GFR falls.
distractorRationale.b: This raises both blood flow and GFR, not a fall in blood flow.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: raised downstream resistance backs pressure up in the glomerulus (GFR rises) while total flow falls.
distractorRationale.d: This lowers PGC and GFR while raising blood flow.

questions.explanation: Constricting the efferent arteriole increases resistance downstream of the glomerular capillaries, so PGC rises and GFR increases. The same resistance rise reduces renal blood flow, so filtration fraction increases.

questions.stem: Describe how the kidney keeps GFR nearly constant when mean arterial pressure varies between about 80 and 180 mmHg. Name the two mechanisms and explain where each acts.
markingGuide: States that autoregulation maintains renal blood flow and GFR over roughly 80 to 180 mmHg mean arterial pressure
Names the myogenic response: afferent arteriolar smooth muscle contracts when stretched by rising pressure
Explains that this raises afferent resistance and prevents a rise in glomerular capillary pressure (and the reverse when pressure falls)
Names tubuloglomerular feedback involving the macula densa of the distal tubule
Explains that increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa signals afferent arteriolar constriction (adenosine), reducing GFR
States that GFR falls with pressure outside the autoregulatory range
questions.explanation: The myogenic response lets afferent arterioles constrict directly when pressure stretches them, buffering PGC. Tubuloglomerular feedback adds a second layer: if GFR rises, more sodium chloride reaches the macula densa, which signals the adjacent afferent arteriole to constrict and return GFR towards normal.

questions.stem: Describe the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier and explain how size and charge together determine why albumin is filtered only in very small amounts.
markingGuide: Names the glomerular basement membrane (type IV collagen, heparan sulfate proteoglycans)
Names the podocyte foot processes and slit diaphragms
States that the basement membrane and other layers carry a negative charge that repels anionic proteins such as albumin
States that the slit diaphragm and basement membrane restrict large molecules by size (albumin is about 66 kDa)
Concludes that damage to charge or podocyte structure produces albuminuria or proteinuria
questions.explanation: The endothelium blocks cells, the basement membrane restricts by size and by negative charge, and the podocyte slit diaphragms form the final size barrier. Albumin is both large and negatively charged, so it is held back by size and repelled by charge, and loss of either property leads to proteinuria.

questions.stem: Explain why creatinine clearance can be used to estimate GFR, and give two limitations of this estimate.
markingGuide: Creatinine is produced at a roughly constant rate by muscle
It is freely filtered at the glomerulus
It is not reabsorbed and only slightly secreted, so excretion approximately equals the amount filtered
States the formula clearance = urine concentration x urine flow / plasma concentration
Limitation: tubular secretion makes it overestimate true GFR slightly

Limitation: serum creatinine depends on muscle mass, so it may be misleadingly low in frail or small people, or relatively insensitive to early GFR loss because of its inverse, non-linear relationship to GFR
questions.explanation: Because creatinine is freely filtered and almost all of what is filtered is excreted, the volume of plasma cleared of creatinine per minute approximates the GFR. The estimate is imperfect because of small tubular secretion and because plasma levels depend on muscle mass and change inversely with GFR.
